\begin{abstract}
Formal methods is pivotal for verifying the reliability of critical systems through rigorous mathematical proofs. However, its adoption is hindered by labor-intensive manual proofs and the expertise required to use theorem provers. Recent advancements in large language models (LLMs) offer new opportunities for automated theorem proving. Two promising approaches are generating tactics step by step and generating a whole proof directly with an LLM. However, existing work makes no attempt to combine the two approaches. 
In this work, we introduce \prover, a dual-model proof synthesis framework that combines tactic-based generation and whole-proof synthesis to harness the benefits of both approaches. \prover\ generates whole proof candidates for evaluation directly, then extracts proof sketches from those candidates. It then uses a tactic-based generation model that integrates automated tools to complete the sketches via stepwise refinement. We implement \prover\ for the Isabelle theorem prover and fine-tune LLMs on our optimized Isabelle datasets. Evaluation on the miniF2F dataset illustrates \prover's effectiveness. We achieve a 59.4\% success rate on miniF2F, where the previous SOTA is 56.1\%. Our ablation studies show that this SOTA result is attributable to combining whole-proof and tactic-based generation. Additionally, we show how the dataset quality, training parameters, and sampling diversity affect the final result during automated theorem proving with LLMs. All of our code, datasets, and LLMs are open source.

\end{abstract}


\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

The field of formal methods plays a pivotal role in ensuring the reliability of critical systems across mathematics, computer science, and engineering~\cite{formalmethods}. It rigorously verifies system correctness through formal specification and math-based proof. However, the labor-intensive nature of manual proof construction and the expertise required for the effective use of interactive theorem provers (ITPs) present significant barriers to widespread adoption. To address this challenge, automated theorem proving has emerged as a paradigm to streamline formal verification~\cite{barrett2011cvc4,de2008z3,groom2018vampire,schulz2002brainiac,weidenbach1996spass}, but its large proof-search space and limited adaptability to diverse proof scenarios have constrained its practicality. 

Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have opened new frontiers for automated theorem proving. Generating proofs is similar to code generation, where LLMs have shown outstanding capabilities \cite{chen2021codex,jiang2024surveylargelanguagemodels}. Moreover, formal proofs are written in formal languages that can be verified by ITPs, e.g., Isabelle/HOL \cite{nipkow2002isabelle}, Rocq \cite{sozeau2025correct}, Lean \cite{moura2021lean}, and HOL Light \cite{harrison1996hol}. Thus, the dangers of LLM hallucinations can be significantly reduced in this process.

In this work, we introduce \prover, an LLM-driven automated theorem-proving framework.
Before \prover, two predominant approaches had emerged 
for LLM-driven automated theorem-proving:
(1) whole-proof synthesis that produces complete formal proof attempts \cite{xin2024deepseek,first2023baldur,wang2024theoremllama}, and (2) tactic-based generation that guides LLMs stepwise \cite{yang2023leandojo,zhao2024subgoalxl,jiang2023draft,polu2020generative}. 
%Tactic-based generation is good at proving each small goal, but does not have an overall proof sketch. 
Whole-proof synthesis excels at high-level planning, but is error-prone at the level of details; tactic-based generation excels at the details, but may struggle with higher-level planning.
\prover\ is the first system that we are aware of to combine these two approaches. In doing so, \prover\ gets the best of both worlds---with state-of-the-art (SOTA) results to show for it.

\prover\ achieves this by employing a dual-model architecture: First, \prover\ uses a whole-proof synthesis model to generate candidate proofs based on the user-provided theorem statement. If any of these candidates are correct whole proofs, then \prover\ is done. Otherwise, \prover\ mechanically abstracts details from those candidate proofs to build proof sketches---abstract proof plans with subgoals in which the detailed tactics are omitted. 
\prover\ uses the ITP to check the proof sketch to ensure its correctness. Finally, \prover\ uses a tactic-based generation model to refine the proof sketch with tactic details and produce a correct whole proof, checked by the ITP.

%By combining these two approaches with the proof sketch as the bridge, \prover\ is able to generate high-level proof plans or sketches that suffice, and then fill in the details of those sketches with the correct details. 
In this way, \prover\ uses the notion of a proof sketch to bridge the gap between the two approaches.
As a consequence, the core ideas of \prover\ can be used to compose \emph{any} whole-proof synthesis model with \emph{any} tactic-based generation model for the same target ITP.
%, so long as some notion of a proof sketch can be conceived.
This is in contrast with prior work generating
proof sketches and filling in the details~\cite{jiang2022thor,jiang2023draft,mikula2023magnushammer,yang2023leandojo},
which does not offer a way to repurpose existing whole-proof synthesis models to generate proof sketches.
%In \prover, there is no need to use a separate model to generate a proof sketch. 
Nonetheless, \prover\ can also take advantage of the benefits of these prior works by integrating hammers~\cite{blanchette2016hammering}, existing tools that automate the proving of simple theorems using symbolic techniques.

While the ideas for \prover\ can be implemented for many ITPs, we focus on Isabelle/HOL \cite{nipkow2002isabelle},
using Sledgehammer~\cite{PAAR-2010:Three_Years_Experience_with} as the hammer. We choose Isabelle both because of the unique challenges that it presents for LLM-based proof synthesis,
as well as the unique advantages that it provides for
curating an optimized dataset (see Section~\ref{gen_inst}).
We evaluate \prover\ on miniF2F~\cite{zheng2022minif2f}, a popular mathematical theorem proving dataset. We improve the SOTA
on miniF2F from 56.1\% to 59.4\%. We show that the combination of whole-proof synthesis and tactic-based generation improves the proof performance. With the integration of hammers, \prover\  performs even better. 
%We also illustrate that refining the proof sketch step-by-step from a whole proof brings a 10\% improvement on miniF2F. 
Additional ablation studies show how the dataset quality, training parameters, and sampling diversity affect the final proof result. We open-source our optimized Isabelle datasets and fine-tuned LLMs on Huggingface. We also provide the source code for \prover.


\paragraph{Contributions:}
\begin{itemize}
    \item[(1)] We propose \prover, an LLM-driven automated theorem proving framework that combines whole-proof synthesis and tactic-based generation, using proof sketches as a bridge between the two approaches to get the best of both worlds. 
    \item[(2)] We implement \prover\ for Isabelle/HOL,
    fine-tuning LLMs on our custom-optimized Isabelle datasets.
    Our evaluation shows that \prover\ brings the SOTA results on miniF2F for Isabelle up from 56.1\% to 59.4\%.
    \item[(3)] Our ablation studies show the effectiveness of \prover\ and how the data quality, training parameters, and sampling diversity affect LLM's ability in theorem proving. 
\end{itemize}






\section{Background: why Isabelle?}
\label{gen_inst}

We implement \prover\ to automate formal proof in the Isabelle ITP. ITPs like Isabelle \cite{nipkow2002isabelle}, Rocq \cite{sozeau2025correct}, and Lean \cite{moura2021lean} are specialized systems that make it possible to formally prove software systems and mathematical theorems.
They rigorously check these formal proofs using
small, trustworthy logic checkers~\cite{nipkow2002isabelle,pierce2010softwarefoundation}.
%This ensures that the proof is actually correct.
Unfortunately, using these ITPs requires substantial work~\cite{klein2009sel4,gu2016certikos,leroy2016compcert}. Complementary tools called automated theorem provers (ATPs) take a different approach of full automation (CVC4 \cite{barrett2011cvc4}, Z3 \cite{de2008z3}, Vampire \cite{groom2018vampire}, E \cite{schulz2002brainiac}, SPASS \cite{weidenbach1996spass}). However, the applicability of ATPs is limited, as they typically use just first-order logic, and they face search-space explosion. Hence, ITPs are useful for expressiveness and scalability. Automated theorem proving with LLMs promises to make ITPs more accessible without compromising on this expressiveness and scalability.

Isabelle is a popular ITP that
%that allows both natural language and mathematical formulas to be expressed rigorously in a formal language. 
widely applied to the formalization of mathematical proofs and formal verification \cite{hales2015formalproofkeplerconjecture,goderisabelle,klein2009sel4,zhao2017refinement}, including proving the correctness of computer hardware or software and proving properties of programming languages and protocols. The most popular instance of Isabelle is Isabelle/HOL, which provides an expressive higher-order logic for complex systems. We use Isabelle/HOL and write it as Isabelle in the rest of this paper for simplicity.
Our choice of Isabelle as a target ITP addresses its unique challenges while also taking advantage of its unique benefits.

\paragraph{Challenges of targeting Isabelle: broad use cases}
%To demonstrate the effectiveness and usability of our framework, we instantiate it with the popular ITP, Isabelle/HOL, and its Sledgehammer \cite{PAAR-2010:Three_Years_Experience_with}, which is the hammer's implementation specifically in Isabelle. 
Targeting Isabelle presents unique challenges compared to other ITPs like Lean.
%further highlighting the adaptability of our framework. 
More work uses LLMs for Lean and gets better results on miniF2F than for Isabelle, because Lean is mainly used for mathematics, with the largest math library (mathlib~\cite{moura2021lean}), and miniF2F is a mathematical benchmark suite.  %extracted from math Olympiad competitions. 
In contrast, Isabelle users tend to focus more on system verification. In system verification, proofs of correctness vary significantly for different implementations, and for different notions of correctness specific to those systems.
%Besides, proving theorems in Isabelle/HOL often requires many premises. An average of 5 premises for one theorem are used in Isabelle's libraries. 

Isabelle has the largest formal proof dataset of high quality with 200K more theorems, compared to Lean's 140K and Rocq's 71K \cite{drori2025diverseinferenceverificationadvanced,reichel2023proof}. This dataset is both an asset and a burden. To its credit, this dataset covers many fields, including mathematical proof, software verification, and programming languages.
%Isabelle's Dataset is highly centralized and of good quality \cite{reichel2023proof}.
However, proofs can vary significantly by field, and it can be challenging for LLMs to learn a common proof pattern to solve proofs across these different fields.

\paragraph{Advantages of targeting Isabelle: two proof styles}
There are two styles of proof in Isabelle.
This may appear to complicate things even further, but it ends up being our greatest asset and a major benefit to targeting Isabelle. The two styles are (1) apply-style proofs \cite{IsabelleTutorial} and (2) Isar proofs \cite{IsarRef}. Both styles employ deductive reasoning. Apply-style proofs emphasize incremental tactic application, where a tactic is a primitive proof step that refines the current proof state to an updated state. Apply-style proofs use tactics step-by-step and reach the conclusion from the initial assumptions. In contrast, Isar proofs are written in Isar, a high-level proof language that provides a structured, human-readable framework for writing formal proofs akin to mathematical proofs. Isar has been designed to make proofs easy to read and to better align with people's ways of thinking and proving \cite{IsarRef}.

\begin{mylisting}[listing options={language=Isabelle}]{Isar and apply-style proof example}
theorem list_reverse: "rev (rev xs) = xs"
|\ttfamily\color{skyblue}Isar proof:|                         |\ttfamily\color{skyblue}apply-style proof:|
    proof (induction xs)                apply (induction xs)
    case Nil                            apply auto
    then show ?case by simp             done
    next
    case (Cons a xs)
    then show ?case by simp
    qed
\end{mylisting}
Listing \ref{listing:1} shows two Isabelle proofs of the same theorem, which states that reversing a list twice does not change the list. In the apply-style proof (right), we first apply induction on the list \textit{xs}, then we use a tactic \textit{auto} in Isabelle to finish the proof. The keyword \textit{done} marks the end of the proof. This proof style is concise, but to understand what these tactics are doing, we need to check the proof state of each step in Isabelle. In the Isar proof (left), we first apply induction on list \textit{xs} that clearly splits the goals into two cases, i.e., case \textit{Nil} and case \textit{Cons a xs}. Here \textit{Nil} means the empty list, and \textit{Cons} means appending an element \textit{a} to the front of the original list \textit{xs}. 

%We fine-tune the whole-proof synthesis model and proofstep model with the optimized datasets. 


Note that these two styles of proofs can be combined, with Isar sketching the final proof while apply-style tactics discharge the remaining subgoals to fill in the sketch. 
For example, for the proof in Listing~\ref{listing:1}, a user could write a proof sketch in Isar by writing \textit{sorry} instead of \textit{by simp}---telling Isabelle to assume the subgoal is correct. Then, after using Isabelle to check that the proof sketch is sufficient, users can fill in the details to finish the proof.
We use this insight to improve our automation, splitting our dataset across these two styles to train our two models, using sketches as bridges between styles. 
This combination of styles is a fundamental idea that our work uses to establish a new SOTA.

\subsection{Framework overview}
\label{sec:framework}
Our framework is depicted in \cref{fig:overview}. The workflow can be divided into the following steps:

\textbf{Step 1:} The input of \prover\ is the user-provided theorem statement. The example \textit{list\_reverse} along with the subsequent proofs here is the same as Listing \ref{listing:1}. Then it will be concatenated with our prompt template (Listing \ref{listing:prompt}) and sent to the \textbf{whole-proof synthesis model}, a fine-tuned LLM.


\textbf{Step 2:} The whole-proof synthesis model will generate $n$ initial candidate proofs at once, where bad proof results are immediately abandoned by the \textbf{proof filter}. Specifically, we write proof patterns in the proof filter to make sure that the Isabelle proof is syntactically correct. If the response is not in a JSON format that we require or does not begin with keywords in Isabelle, it must be wrong. Then the syntax-correct proofs will be evaluated by the \textbf{checker}, i.e., the Isabelle theorem prover.
The initial candidate proof in \cref{fig:overview} is syntax-correct but fails to pass the checker because the tactic \textit{by presburger} for the first subgoal is wrong.
The synthesis and evaluation of $n$ proofs are both fast due to the concurrency support in \prover. We set $n$ to be 128 in our experiments. If one of the proofs passes the checker, we provide the final whole proof with the theorem to the user.

\textbf{Step 3:} If none of the $n$ proofs are correct, we use a \textbf{sketch builder} to reconstruct those syntax-correct proofs that pass the proof filter. The detailed proof steps will be hidden while only a proof sketch is left. Unlike previous work, we directly generate proof sketches mechanically from candidate proofs. 
%without having to train another LLM for generating sketches.
%The proof sketch builder makes the workflow concise because we do not need to train another LLM to generate proof sketches. 
Specifically, we substitute all proof tactics for each subgoal with the keyword \textit{sorry} in Isabelle. The checker will assume the subgoal is correct when it meets \textit{sorry}. An example of a proof sketch is shown in \cref{fig:overview}. Then we evaluate these proof sketches in Isabelle \textbf{checker} and filter out incorrect sketches, e.g., using a nonexistent proof method in the beginning. Most of the sketches are correct without detailed proof steps. Again, this process is very fast due to concurrency support. 

\textbf{Step 4:} Subsequently, we use a \textbf{tactic-based generation model} to find proof steps for each subgoal in one proof sketch. It is composed of a fine-tuned LLM for proof steps and Sledgehammer with heuristics in Isabelle. It also generates $n$ possible responses for each subgoal. This model focuses on generating proofs for small subgoals, while the whole-proof synthesis model focuses on generating whole proofs with premises.
Premises are auxiliary lemmas for proving the final theorem. Existing work selects premises in two ways. 
%Because premises are too large to fit into LLMs as input due to context length limitations. There are two ways to solve this problem. 
The first one is to build a premise library and retrieve related premises based on the theorem input~\cite{wang2024lego,yang2023leandojo}. Another way is to train the model to memorize premises and learn to use them when similar theorems appear~\cite{first2023baldur}. We choose the second method and require our whole-proof synthesis model to do premise selection.

\textbf{Step 5:} Then we use a \textbf{proof refinement builder} to refine \textit{sorry} with generated proof steps and send the whole proof to Isabelle. The output of the refinement builder is the same as the final whole proof. As shown in \cref{fig:overview}, all instances of the keyword \textit{sorry} in the proof sketch are replaced with specific proof steps, i.e., \textit{by simp}. If the candidate proof does not pass the \textbf{checker}, the refinement builder will refine the proof sketch with other proof steps from the tactic-based generation model. 
Finally, we provide the proof result to the user. The algorithm of \prover\ is shown in \cref{alg:atp}.

\begin{algorithm}[H]
\caption{HybridProver workflow}
\label{alg:atp}
\begin{algorithmic}[1]
\Require User provided theorem $L$, prompt template $T$
\Ensure Valid Isabelle whole proof or failure
\State Generate candidate proofs $\mathcal{P} \gets \text{LLM}_{\text{whole}}(L,T)$ 
\Comment{\textbf{Step 1: Initial candidate proof synthesis}}
\State Filter syntax-correct proofs $\mathcal{P}_{\text{syntax}} \gets proof\_filter (\mathcal{P})$ \label{line:filter}
\Comment{\textbf{Step 2: Filter proofs and check}}

\State $\mathcal{P}_{\text{valid}} \gets \emptyset$
\State \textbf{parallel for} $p \in \mathcal{P}_{\text{syntax}}$ \textbf{do}
\State \quad \textbf{if} $\text{check}(p, L) = \texttt{True}$ \textbf{then} $\mathcal{P}_{\text{valid}} \gets \mathcal{P}_{\text{valid}} \cup \{p\}$
\State \textbf{end parallel for}

\If{$\mathcal{P}_{\text{valid}} \neq \emptyset$} 
    \State \Return \textbf{any} $p \in \mathcal{P}_{\text{valid}}$
\EndIf

\State Generate sketches $\mathcal{S} \gets \{\text{replaceTacticsWithSorry}(p) \mid p \in \mathcal{P}\}$ \label{line:sketch}
\Comment{\textbf{Step 3: Build proof sketch}}
\State \textbf{parallel} verify $\mathcal{S}_{\text{valid}} \gets \{s \in \mathcal{S} \mid \text{check}(s, L) = \texttt{True}\}$

\State \textbf{parallel for} $s \in \mathcal{S}_{\text{valid}}$ \textbf{do}
\Comment{\textbf{Step 4 \& Step 5: Tactic-based refinement}}
\State \quad Extract subgoals $G_1, \dots, G_n \gets \text{parseSubgoals}(s)$ 
\State \quad Generate tactic proof steps $\mathcal{T} \gets \bigcup_{i=1}^n \left( \text{LLM}_{\text{step}}(G_i) \cup \text{Sledgehammer}(G_i) \right)$ \label{line:tactic}
\State \quad Refine proof sketch $p_{\text{refined}} \gets \text{substituteSorry}(s, \mathcal{T})$
\State \quad \textbf{If} {$\text{IsabelleVerify}(p_{\text{refined}}, L) = \texttt{True}$} 
        \State \quad \quad \Return $p_{\text{refined}}$ 
\State \textbf{end parallel for}

\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}

\subsection{Dataset optimization}
\label{sec:datasetoptimization}

%We extract Isabelle2021's HOL library and AFP-2021-10-22 as training data on Isabelle. After data purification, we split the whole dataset into two training datasets, 


We extract Isabelle datasets using the PISA environment \cite{jiang2021lisa}.
%We fine-tune the whole-proof synthesis model and proofstep model with the optimized datasets. 
Then, we purify the data because the original data will largely mislead the LLM. Specifically, we purify extra blanks and tabs. Then we delete all the comments and rewrite some symbols, e.g., the open and close brackets. Finally, we transform all proofs into a structured output format \textit{\{Isabelle\_proof: proof code\}} for models to learn. 

After data purification, we split the dataset into two datasets depending on the proof style: an Isar proof \cite{IsarRef} dataset to fine-tune the whole-proof synthesis model and an apply-style proof \cite{IsabelleTutorial} dataset to fine-tune the LLM in the tactic-based generation model. We further analyze the number of proof steps for each theorem and filter out some theorems. Specifically, we find that an apply-style proof generally has 1-5 proof steps and an Isar proof has 11-30 proof steps. We filter out theorems that exceed 5 steps in apply-style proofs to keep the tactic-based generation model focused on finding concise proofs of details. We also filter out theorems that are more than 50 or fewer than 5 proof steps, because they are either too simple or too complex for the model to learn proof sketches.

\section{Experiments}
\label{sec:experiment}

We first introduce the setup for \prover\ (\cref{sec:setup}), including the dataset, the interactive environment with Isabelle, and the experimental setup. Then, we show the main results to demonstrate the effectiveness of \prover\ in establishing a new SOTA (\cref{sec:results}). Finally, we describe additional ablation studies (\cref{sec:ablation}) to answer four questions, with the following takeaways:

\begin{itemize}
\item[1)] The more similar an LLM-generated proof pattern is to the training data, the higher the quality of the proof. 

\item[2)] The quality of the data, the learning rate, and the number of epochs do affect the results, while the number of parameters in LoRA has a trivial impact.

\item[3)] Sampling diversity impacts the result. The sampling temperature should be moderate, and a higher sampling rate brings a higher success rate.

\item[4)] Providing premises, few-shot examples, and labels has a trivial impact on improving the miniF2F success rate.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Setup}
\label{sec:setup}

\paragraph{Dataset}
We extract and optimize Isabelle libraries (\cref{sec:datasetoptimization}) as the training datasets, with the help of PISA \cite{jiang2021lisa}. These datasets are used to train the whole-proof synthesis model and the tactic-based generation model separately. PISA includes the Isabelle/HOL library and the Archive of Formal Proofs (AFP) with version 2021-10-22. The former is more foundational, with around 70K theorems. The latter is a proof library contributed by most Isabelle researchers, with around 170K theorems. It diverges from mathematical problems to formal verification of software and hardware. We follow the same configurations of prior works \cite{jiang2021lisa,jiang2022thor,jiang2023draft} and split AFP theorems into 95\%/1\%/4\% for the training/validation/test sets. The Isabelle/HOL library is classified in the training dataset because it might be used by the AFP theorems.


We choose miniF2F \cite{zheng2022minif2f} as our evaluation dataset because it is %popular and 
used in many research studies \cite{yang2023leandojo,jiang2023draft,zhao2024subgoalxl}. It is an open-source collection containing 488 high school math competition problems. These problems are divided into two groups: 244 for validation and 244 for final testing. All problems have been translated into 4 proof assistant languages: Lean, HOL light, Metamath, and Isabelle. Since we do not use the validation set during training, we use only the test set for our experiments. 
%MiniF2F might be pretrained on some LLMs

%While miniF2F \cite{zheng2022minif2f} is the only cross-system benchmark in the theorem-proving field, it exhibits two limitations. It does not have enough theorems for training and is restricted to the domain of olympiad-style math problems, which is not equal to the ability in theorem proving. Therefore, we also use the PISA \cite{jiang2021lisa} dataset for training and evaluation.


\paragraph{Interactive environment}
We interact with Isabelle using Isabelle-client \cite{10.1007/978-3-031-16681-5_24}. It is a Python client library that strictly follows the Isabelle system manual \cite{wenzel2021isabelle}. We use one server, one client, and multiple sessions for concurrency. \textit{watchdog\_timeout} is set to 30s for evaluation. Evaluation in Isabelle is time-consuming even for a small sampling rate and a small dataset. It costs 300 CPU hours to evaluate 244 theorems in miniF2F with a 32 sampling rate for one LLM. Thus, we do ablation studies with a relatively low sampling rate and small timeout. To set up Sledgehammer, we follow the default Isabelle2021 configuration \cite{jiang2021lisa}, where the Sledgehammer timeout limit is 30s, with the on-machine five default ATPs (E, SPASS, Vampire, Z3, and CVC4). 
We also complement Sledgehammer with 11 heuristics for proofs: \textit{['by auto', 'by simp', 'by blast', 'by fastforce', 'by force', 'by eval', 'by presburger', 'by sos', 'by arith', 'by linarith', 'by (auto simp: field\_simps)']}. 
%We ask Sledgehammer to generate Isar proofs for each lemma.



\paragraph{Experimental setup}
In initial small-model experiments, we generated proofs using more than 15 different open-source models. In the end, we chose Qwen-Coder-14B as our base model for further training because it had the highest proof success rate. For LLM fine-tuning, we use 8 Nvidia A40 GPUs. Fine-tuning our model with the whole optimized Isabelle dataset and 3 epochs takes 200 GPU hours. The cost of ablation studies for other LLMs and configurations is not included. We use LoRA \cite{hu2022lora} to train around 1\% of all parameters with a \textit{lora\_rank} 32 and all target layers open for adjustment.  
In the first 10\% of steps, the learning rate warms up linearly from 0 to the maximum value $e^{-5}$. Then it decays to 0 following a cosine schedule. The context length for the training data is 2048 tokens, and the total batch size is 64.
%For evaluation data, we do the same random sampling from PISA's test theorems that cover most libraries, as existing works do. Thus, the evaluation dataset will not be exactly the same. Besides, the growth of formal Isabelle libraries is slow with 20K theorems increase per year comparing to the whole 240K theorems. Therefore, the evaluation result in Isabelle2021 is also meaningful and scalable to the updated libraries. 
For evaluation, we use a 128-core Intel CPU with 256GB RAM while setting the concurrent processes to 64. The whole evaluation process cost nearly 10,000 CPU hours.

To illustrate how each component in \prover\ affects the final result, we run experiments on variants of our framework (\cref{tab:model training}). The whole-proof synthesis model alone achieves 37.7\%, while the tactic-based generation model alone achieves 34.8\%. With a simple combination of the two models (the union of results), the success rate is 41.4\%. In miniF2F, some theorems are simple and only need one proof step. However, the whole-proof synthesis model generates verbose and incorrect Isar proofs for those theorems. Thus, the tactic-based generation model can help with such theorems. Sledgehammer with heuristics slightly improves the success rate of the model by around 2\%, which means the tactic-based LLM can cover most theorems that the hammer could prove.

\subsection{Additional ablation studies}
\label{sec:ablation}

\paragraph{Is the proof pattern similarity equal to the proof quality?}
During the fine-tuning stage, we try to feed the model enough theorem-proof pairs. The LLM learns to generate proof patterns similar to the training data. But is the proof pattern similarity equal to the quality? Thus, we not only test the success rate of the miniF2F dataset, but also record all responses from the sampling during the whole evaluation. We make a comparison between them and find that generally, the higher the total correct response is, the higher the success rate for all theorems is. It demonstrates that proof pattern similarity is strongly relevant to the proof quality, reflecting the improvement from training.


\paragraph{How do data quality and training parameters affect fine-tuning effects?}
We use the original Qwen-Coder-7B to build our baseline for computing source restrictions. The original model has difficulty following our instructions because it is only a generically pretrained model. So we prompt the model and additionally enforce a structured output format for the original model's responses. We try fine-tuning on variants of our optimized Isabelle dataset with different hyperparameter combinations, i.e., learning rate, lora\_rank, and number of epochs. We generate responses with the same prompt, as shown in Listing \ref{listing:prompt}.
We find that the quality of data, learning rate, and number of epochs do affect the results.
%In the training process, we have done experiments based on Qwen-Coder-7B to study what affects the quality of fine-tuning. 
These heuristics can be takeaways to researchers using LLMs for similar tasks.  If we fine-tune the model with original data, the model's output is deeply polluted by useless tokens and tabs. The LLM will also output a lot of meaningless tokens in the responses. After data purification described in \cref{sec:datasetoptimization}, the model's pass rate on miniF2F improves at least 10\%. For epochs, we find that 3 epochs is the best compared to 1, 6, and 10 epochs. More training will only lead to overfitting. Besides, the type of theorems in the training data varies from math to software and systems, while miniF2F is only about math. For learning rate, we tried $e^{-4}, 5e^{-5}, e^{-5}, 5e^{-6}, e^{-6}$, and $5e^{-7}$ with a warm-up and cosine schedule. We find that the best is $e^{-5}$. Moreover, we tried different lora ranks, including 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256. Here, a rank 32 modifies around 0.92\% of the full parameters in an LLM. However, we find that the lora\_rank is almost irrelevant to the results.


\paragraph{Does sampling diversity impact the results?}
After we have a fine-tuned model, we can choose different sampling parameters for response generation, e.g., sampling temperature $T$ and sampling rate. For proof generation tasks, the model is asked to be stable enough to generate formatted and syntactically correct responses. Thus, $T$ is typically set to 0.2-0.5. However, existing works sample multiple responses for one theorem, and a higher $T$ can improve the possibility of success. For example, LISA uses a $T$ = 1.0 and Thor uses $T$ = 1.2. Sampling rate @32 means that if any response in the 32 generated ones for one theorem passes the evaluation, the theorem is true. In our work, we performed an ablation study on a fine-tuned Qwen-Coder-7B model, where $T$ ranges from 0.3 to 1.2 and sampling rate from @32 to @128. The results are shown in \cref{tab:pisa_success}. We can infer that $T$ does affect the sampling result. Set $T$ from 0.6 to 0.9 is moderate, where a higher or lower temperature will decrease the success rate. We analyze the error messages returned from Isabelle and find that the model hallucinates many inexisted facts when $T$ is too high. We also infer that a higher sampling rate (@128) can bring 4\% more improvement.

Most theorems in the Isabelle library require pre-defined premises to prove. Thus, we provide theorems with premises in the training data as input, where the output is the proof. We ask the model to learn how to find relevant premises from the library and how to build proofs based on these premises. Then we record all the error messages and notice that \textit{undefined fact} error decreases 50\%, meaning that the model has learned not to hallucinate nonexistent premises. However, the improvement on the miniF2F dataset is trivial. The reason is that most miniF2F theorems require no premises. For few-shot prompting, we construct three classical examples covering a simple apply-style proof, an apply-style induction proof, and an Isar proof. For the label, we mark each theorem with the file path it belongs to so that the model can learn the big category of this theorem. For example, if a theorem belongs to a \textit{List} theory file in Isabelle, the model will learn to find premises in the \textit{List} file first. 
However, the improvement is still trivial in the miniF2F because these theorems all belong to the mathematical category.

\section{Related work}
\label{headings}

\paragraph{Interactive theorem proving.}
Theorem proving is widely used for ensuring the safety and security of critical software and systems. Most work in interactive theorem proving involves some manual proof construction by human experts, a process that is labor-intensive and time-consuming. %Their efforts are often counted in person-years.
%For example, in verifying the correctness and security of a complete and general-purpose microkernel in Isabelle/HOL, the seL4 team~\cite{klein2009sel4} takes 30 person-years to formally specify and prove 8700 lines of C code. 
For example, the seL4 team \cite{klein2009sel4} takes 30 person-years to verify a general-purpose microkernel with 8700 lines of C code in Isabelle.
The CertiKOS team \cite{gu2016certikos} verifies a concurrent OS through deep abstraction layers in Rocq \cite{gu2015deep,gu2018certified}.
%, which simplifies the proof obligations. 
They take 3 person-years to prove 6500 lines of C and x86 assembly. 
%Zhao et al. take 1 person-year to verify the security of an ARINC653-compliant separation kernel through refinement, which lowers the proof burden.
CompCert \cite{leroy2016compcert} is the first formally verified C compiler to be exempt from miscompilation. Six person-years are taken in Rocq to construct proofs.
Additionally, most theorem-proving works in other operating systems take more than 1 person-year \cite{sigurbjarnarson2016push,shinde2020besfs,chajed2019verifying,zhao2017refinement,amani2016cogent,proverit_hu,verbeek2015formal}.
%e.g., Yggdrasil \cite{sigurbjarnarson2016push}, BesFS \cite{shinde2020besfs}, Perennial \cite{chajed2019verifying}, ARINC653 \cite{zhao2017refinement}, COGENT \cite{amani2016cogent}, ProveriT \cite{proverit_hu}, and PikeOS \cite{verbeek2015formal}.

\paragraph{LLMs for theorem proving.}
The use of LLMs to automate theorem proving was pioneered by Polu and Sutskever \cite{polu2020generative}. 
%Subsequent research efforts have focused on either improving the reasoning capabilities of LLM-based systems or extending their functionality to support ITPs, which previously lay beyond their scope. 
Subsequent work has focused on improving the reasoning capabilities of LLM-based systems.
Open-source interactive environments like
Leandojo~\cite{yang2023leandojo} for Lean, and PISA \cite{jiang2021lisa} and Isabelle-client \cite{10.1007/978-3-031-16681-5_24} for Isabelle, make it easier to build LLM-based tools for automated theorem proving.
%We use PISA to extract datasets and make some optimizations to better train LLMs. We also make our framework concurrent and fast with the support of Isabelle-client. 
Likewise, open-source datasets and benchmarks like miniF2F \cite{zheng2022minif2f} and Proofnet \cite{azerbayev2023proofnet} provide the basis for evaluation.
%These open-source environments and datasets facilitate the LLM applications in theorem proving. 
Automation often uses premise selection prior to proof generation
to find relevant premises~\cite{yang2023leandojo,jiang2022thor,wang2024lego,mikula2023magnushammer}. For example, LEGO \cite{wang2024lego} builds a growing library and retrieves premises from it, while Thor \cite{jiang2022thor} delegates premise selection to hammers during the proving process. In \prover, we ask both the fine-tuned LLM and Sledgehammer in Isabelle to perform premise selection. 
%LLMs can find premises that appear most of the time in the training dataset, and Sledgehammer can find relevant premises by its algorithms and heuristics.
Prior work on LLM-based proof generation also varies by what the
LLM is used for and by its input context.
Some work \cite{yang2023leandojo,zhao2024subgoalxl,jiang2023draft,polu2020generative,lin2024fvel} uses LLMs to generate tactic-based proofs step by step. Other work \cite{xin2024deepseek,first2023baldur,wang2024theoremllama} uses LLMs to generate the whole proof at once. 
For example, Polu \cite{polu2020generative} and FVEL \cite{lin2024fvel} ask LLM to generate the next tactic based on the current proof state. Baldur \cite{first2023baldur} makes LLMs generate whole proofs based on the input theorem. \prover\ organically combines these two approaches and gets a better proof quality.
After the proof generation, some works also focus on proof search that chooses appropriate generated responses with different algorithms, such as Best first search~\cite{polu2020generative,han2022proof,yang2023leandojo}, and Monte Carlo tree search \cite{wang2023dt,lample2022hypertree,xin2024deepseek}.
%, where Deepseek-prover \cite{xin2024deepseek} employs an innovative MCTS algorithm to enhance both the accuracy and diversity of proof generation. 
Despite the improvement, these search algorithms often require additional computational resources that are non-trivial. Besides, a few works try to integrate hammers and sketches to improve the performance \cite{jiang2022thor,jiang2023draft,mikula2023magnushammer,zhao2024subgoalxl,yang2023leandojo}. For instance, DSP \cite{jiang2023draft} generates proof sketches with subgoals and uses hammers to boost the proof success rate. 
%Several works \cite{zhao2024subgoalxl,yang2023leandojo} require the model to generate sketches and prove subgoals step by step. 
\prover\ differs from them in two aspects. First, we not only integrate hammers but also a fine-tuned LLM trained on our optimized dataset to improve the performance. Second, we build the proof sketch mechanically from the whole proof, which bridges the gap between whole-proof synthesis and tactic-based generation, while DSP builds sketches from informal proofs by prompting another LLM.
%Others utilize error messages from the proof assistant for improving \cite{first2023baldur}.



\paragraph{Autoformalization.}

In this work, we focus on theorem proving where a formal specification already exists. Another interesting area is autoformalization, where researchers translate natural language texts into formal specifications and proofs  \cite{azerbayev2023proofnet,wang2018first,cosler2023nl2spec,hahn2022formal,wu2022autoformalization,chen2023nl2tl}. 
%For example, Proofnet \cite{azerbayev2023proofnet} leverages the few-shot learning capabilities of pre-trained language models, using prompts to guide the model in transforming natural language text descriptions into formalized specifications. 
The amount of natural language texts and mathematical proofs is far greater than formal texts. Therefore, autoformalization creates a lot of high-quality data used for model training, which solves the data scarcity problem. Other works also try to generate specifications based on code \cite{wen2024enchanting,cosler2023nl2spec,si2018learning,si2020code2inv}. 
%For example, AutoSpec \cite{cosler2023nl2spec} automatically generates formalized specifications from C code that meet formal verification requirements.


\section{Conclusion and future work}
\label{sec:discussion}
 %Automated theorem proving significantly reduces the proof burden in theorem proving by reducing the need for manually writing proofs, a persistent bottleneck in the large-scale application of formal methods. 
We introduced \prover, an LLM-driven proof synthesis framework for automated theorem proving. \prover's power comes from a novel combination of whole-proof synthesis and tactic-based generation with the help of hammers, using stepwise refinement of proof sketches as the bridge between the two approaches. 
%It generates proof sketches and completes them with stepwise refinement. 
Our implementation of \prover\ for the Isabelle theorem prover achieves a SOTA result of 59.4\% accuracy on the widely-used miniF2F dataset, surpassing the previous SOTA of 56.4\% for Isabelle.
%Ablation studies further show that dataset quality, training parameters, and sampling diversity affect the quality of synthesized proofs. 

One limitation of \prover\ is that it uses a simple proof search method during the proof sketch refinement. When the number of subgoals inside the proof sketches grows, the refinement and evaluation process will be very slow. 
In the future, we plan to integrate proof search into our tactic-based generation model to make it more efficient. We also plan to use extended pretraining and reinforcement learning to further improve the quality of LLM-generated proofs. Finally, we plan to develop an integrated tool that is easy to use.

\section{Technical Appendices and Supplementary Material}
\label{appendix}
\subsection{Hammers}
We integrate hammers in our framework to augment theorem proving.
Blanchette et al. \cite{blanchette2016hammering} define hammers as methods that ``automate reasoning over large libraries developed with formal proof assistants.'' Most ITPs have their own hammers, e.g., Coqhammer in Rocq and Sledgehammer in Isabelle. Sledgehammer in Isabelle is the most powerful one \cite{PAAR-2010:Three_Years_Experience_with}. Providing the input theorem, Sledgehammer first finds relevant premises using machine learning and a traditional filtering algorithm \cite{PAAR-2010:Three_Years_Experience_with}. Then it translates the input theorem together with a heuristic selection of hundreds of premises into goals that external ATPs can recognize. 
Then, ATPs solve these problems and return the results to Sledgehammer. Sledgehammer thus gets the useful premises and finally reconstructs proofs for the Isabelle trusted kernel to check. 
Every ITP has a trusted kernel, a minimal and rigorously verified core that checks manually constructed proofs following mathematical logic rules \cite{nipkow2002isabelle,pierce2010softwarefoundation}.
Since the kernel checks these proofs, it is unnecessary for the user to worry about the correctness of the generated proof.

Sledgehammer makes writing proofs convenient. Isabelle users only need to write the assumptions and the final goal that they want to prove. Then users can call Sledgehammer directly to finish the proof. Sledgehammer is good at generating short proofs \cite{PAAR-2010:Three_Years_Experience_with}. Thus, if users also provide a proof sketch with some subgoals introducing how the proof might be done, Sledgehammer will find proofs for each subgoal and construct the whole proof more easily. It is worth mentioning that Sledgehammer does not do induction very well. LLMs might help with theorems that require induction proofs.

title: Artificial Intelligence, Chaos, Prediction and Understanding in Science
summary:
Machine learning and deep learning techniques are contributing much to the
advancement of science. Their powerful predictive capabilities appear in
numerous disciplines, including chaotic dynamics, but they miss understanding.
The main thesis here is that prediction and understanding are two very
different and important ideas that should guide us about the progress of
science. Furthermore, it is emphasized the important role played by that
nonlinear dynamical systems for the process of understanding. The path of the
future of science will be marked by a constructive dialogue between big data
and big theory, without which we cannot understand.

title: DICE: Discrete inverse continuity equation for learning population dynamics
summary:
We introduce the Discrete Inverse Continuity Equation (DICE) method, a
generative modeling approach that learns the evolution of a stochastic process
from given sample populations at a finite number of time points. Models learned
with DICE capture the typically smooth and well-behaved population dynamics,
rather than the dynamics of individual sample trajectories that can exhibit
complex or even chaotic behavior. The DICE loss function is developed
specifically to be invariant, even in discrete time, to spatially constant but
time-varying spurious constants that can emerge during training; this
invariance increases training stability and robustness. Generating a trajectory
of sample populations with DICE is fast because samples evolve directly in the
time interval over which the stochastic process is formulated, in contrast to
approaches that condition on time and then require multiple sampling steps per
time step. DICE is stable to train, in situations where other methods for
learning population dynamics fail, and DICE generates representative samples
with orders of magnitude lower costs than methods that have to condition on
time. Numerical experiments on a wide range of problems from random waves,
Vlasov-Poisson instabilities and high-dimensional chaos are included to justify
these assertions.

Abstract
Lagrangian turbulence lies at the core of numerous applied and fundamental problems related to the physics of dispersion and mixing in engineering, biofluids, the atmosphere, oceans and astrophysics. Despite exceptional theoretical, numerical and experimental efforts conducted over the past 30 years, no existing models are capable of faithfully reproducing statistical and topological properties exhibited by particle trajectories in turbulence. We propose a machine learning approach, based on a state-of-the-art diffusion model, to generate single-particle trajectories in three-dimensional turbulence at high Reynolds numbers, thereby bypassing the need for direct numerical simulations or experiments to obtain reliable Lagrangian data. Our model demonstrates the ability to reproduce most statistical benchmarks across time scales, including the fat-tail distribution for velocity increments, the anomalous power law and the increased intermittency around the dissipative scale. Slight deviations are observed below the dissipative scale, particularly in the acceleration and flatness statistics. Surprisingly, the model exhibits strong generalizability for extreme events, producing events of higher intensity and rarity that still match the realistic statistics. This paves the way for producing synthetic high-quality datasets for pretraining various downstream applications of Lagrangian turbulence.

bib.author: Bec, J. and Gustavsson, K. and Mehlig, B.
bib.abstract: When very small particles are suspended in a fluid in motion, they tend to follow the flow. How such tracer particles are mixed, transported, and dispersed by turbulent flow has been successfully described by statistical models. Heavy particles, with mass densities larger than that of the carrying fluid, can detach from the flow. This results in preferential sampling, small-scale fractal clustering, and large relative velocities. To describe these effects of particle inertia, one must consider both particle positions and velocities in phase space. In recent years, statistical phase-space models have significantly contributed to our understanding of inertial-particle dynamics in turbulence. These models help to identify the key mechanisms and nondimensional parameters governing the particle dynamics and have made qualitative and, in some cases, quantitative predictions. This article reviews statistical phase-space models for the dynamics of small, yet heavy, spherical particles in turbulence. We evaluate their effectiveness by comparing their predictions with results from numerical simulations and laboratory experiments, and we summarize their successes and failures.

bib.abstract: Energy-Based Models (EBMs), also known as non-normalized probabilistic models, specify probability density or mass functions up to an unknown normalizing constant. Unlike most other probabilistic models, EBMs do not place a restriction on the tractability of the normalizing constant, thus are more flexible to parameterize and can model a more expressive family of probability distributions. However, the unknown normalizing constant of EBMs makes training particularly difficult. Our goal is to provide a friendly introduction to modern approaches for EBM training. We start by explaining maximum likelihood training with Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), and proceed to elaborate on MCMC-free approaches, including Score Matching (SM) and Noise Constrastive Estimation (NCE). We highlight theoretical connections among these three approaches, and end with a brief survey on alternative training methods, which are still under active research. Our tutorial is targeted at an audience with basic understanding of generative models who want to apply EBMs or start a research project in this direction.

bib.abstract: Modern distribution matching algorithms for training diffusion or flow models directly prescribe the time evolution of the marginal distributions between two boundary distributions. In this work, we consider a generalized distribution matching setup, where these marginals are only implicitly described as a solution to some task-specific objective function. The problem setup, known as the Generalized Schr{\textbackslash}"odinger Bridge (GSB), appears prevalently in many scientific areas both within and without machine learning. We propose Generalized Schr{\textbackslash}"odinger Bridge Matching (GSBM), a new matching algorithm inspired by recent advances, generalizing them beyond kinetic energy minimization and to account for task-specific state costs. We show that such a generalization can be cast as solving conditional stochastic optimal control, for which efficient variational approximations can be used, and further debiased with the aid of path integral theory. Compared to prior methods for solving GSB problems, our GSBM algorithm always preserves a feasible transport map between the boundary distributions throughout training, thereby enabling stable convergence and significantly improved scalability. We empirically validate our claims on an extensive suite of experimental setups, including crowd navigation, opinion depolarization, LiDAR manifolds, and image domain transfer. Our work brings new algorithmic opportunities for training diffusion models enhanced with task-specific optimality structures.

title: Algorithmic Analysis of GTFS-RT vehicle position accuracy
summary:
This paper presents three novel algorithms for calculating geodesic
intersections on an ellipsoid. These algorithms are applied in a case study
analyzing real-time transit data in California to assess vehicle position
drift. The analysis reveals that while certain data anomalies can be corrected,
large-scale discrepancies persist. The paper concludes by proposing a set of
practical solutions that can be implemented by either data producers or
consumers to significantly improve positional accuracy.

title: Skillful joint probabilistic weather forecasting from marginals
summary:
Machine learning (ML)-based weather models have rapidly risen to prominence
due to their greater accuracy and speed than traditional forecasts based on
numerical weather prediction (NWP), recently outperforming traditional
ensembles in global probabilistic weather forecasting. This paper presents FGN,
a simple, scalable and flexible modeling approach which significantly
outperforms the current state-of-the-art models. FGN generates ensembles via
learned model-perturbations with an ensemble of appropriately constrained
models. It is trained directly to minimize the continuous rank probability
score (CRPS) of per-location forecasts. It produces state-of-the-art ensemble
forecasts as measured by a range of deterministic and probabilistic metrics,
makes skillful ensemble tropical cyclone track predictions, and captures joint
spatial structure despite being trained only on marginals.

title: Commissioning, characterization and first high dose rate irradiations at a compact X-ray tube for microbeam and minibeam radiation therapy
summary:
Minibeam and microbeam radiation therapy promise improved treatment outcomes
through reduced normal tissue toxicity at better tumor control rates. The lack
of suitable compact radiation sources limits the clinical application of
minibeams to superficial tumors and renders it impossible for microbeams. We
developed and constructed the first prototype of a compact line-focus X-ray
tube (LFXT) with technology potentially suitable for clinical translation of
minibeams and microbeams. We give an overview of the commissioning process
preceding the first operation, present optical and radiological focal spot
characterization methods, and dosimetric measurements. Additionally, we report
on first preclinical in vitro cell and in vivo mouse brain irradiations
conducted with the LFXT prototype. The focal spot characterization resulted in
a strongly eccentric electron distribution with a width of 72.3 $\mu$m.
Dosimetry showed sharp microbeam dose profiles with steep lateral penumbras and
a peak-to-valley dose ratio above 10 throughout a 70 mm thick PMMA phantom. An
open-field dose rate of 4.3 Gy/s was measured at an acceleration voltage of 150
kV and a beam current of 17.4 mA at 150 mm distance from the focal spot. In
vitro and in vivo experiments demonstrated the feasibility of the LFXT for
minibeam and microbeam applications with field sizes of 1.5-2 cm. The mice
displayed no observable side effects throughout the follow-up period after
whole-brain 260 $\mu$m-minibeam irradiation. We successfully constructed and
commissioned the first proof-of-concept LFXT prototype. Dosimetric
characterizations of the achieved microbeam field showed the superiority of the
LFXT compared to conventional X-ray tubes in terms of beam quality. In future
developments, the remaining limitations of the prototype will be addressed for
improved minibeam and first ever microbeam radiation therapy in a clinical
setting.
